title: Inflammatory Gastrointestinal Diseases
subject: Gastrointestinal System (GAST)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains the inflammatory diseases of the digestive tube from the esophagus to the anus: reflux and its complications, the three main forms of esophagitis, acute and chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer, esophageal tears and rupture, appendicitis, diverticular disease, noninfectious enteritis and colitis, inflammatory bowel disease, and common anorectal disorders. Nearly every one follows the same logic. Injury wins when an aggressive force (acid, pepsin, bile, drugs, pressure, bacteria, or the immune system) outweighs mucosal defense or blood supply. Board questions give you the site, the depth of injury, the timing of pain, and a biopsy or imaging finding, and ask you to name the process and predict its complication.
prerequisites: Layers of the gut wall: mucosa, muscularis mucosae, submucosa, muscularis propria, serosa or adventitia
Regulation of gastric acid by gastrin, histamine, acetylcholine, and somatostatin
Prostaglandin synthesis by cyclooxygenase and its mucosal protective effects
Visceral versus somatic pain pathways and dermatomes T5 to T12
Acute inflammation, granulomatous inflammation, metaplasia, and dysplasia

connections.how: Barrett esophagus, H. pylori gastritis, autoimmune gastritis, and long-standing colitis are the inflammatory precursors of adenocarcinoma, MALT lymphoma, and gastric neuroendocrine tumors.
Autoimmune gastritis and ileal Crohn disease cause vitamin B12 deficiency and megaloblastic anemia, while chronic ulcer or NSAID blood loss causes iron deficiency.
Eosinophilic esophagitis is a Th2 allergic disease, Crohn disease a Th1 and Th17 granulomatous disease, and autoimmune gastritis an organ-specific autoimmune disease.
Fat malabsorption in ileal Crohn disease causes calcium oxalate kidney stones and gallstones, and ulcerative colitis is the main association of primary sclerosing cholangitis.
Artery position explains which ulcers bleed, peritoneal innervation explains appendicitis pain, and the dentate line explains which anal lesions hurt.

terms.def: A loss of mucosa that stops above the muscularis mucosae and so heals without a scar.
A defect that extends through the muscularis mucosae into the submucosa or deeper and heals by fibrosis.
Reversible replacement of one mature cell type by another that better tolerates a chronic stress, such as columnar for squamous epithelium in Barrett esophagus.
Disordered growth with cytologic atypia that has not invaded the basement membrane; it is the direct precursor of carcinoma.
Inflammation through the full thickness of the bowel wall, the feature that allows fistulas and strictures in Crohn disease.
An outpouching of mucosa and submucosa only, pushed through a gap in the muscularis propria.
A vagally mediated relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter, not triggered by swallowing, that is the main moment reflux occurs.
Absence of gastric hydrochloric acid secretion, as after parietal cell loss in autoimmune gastritis.
A collection of neutrophils within the lumen of a colonic crypt, typical of active ulcerative colitis.
Free gas in the peritoneal cavity, seen under the diaphragm on an upright film after perforation of a hollow viscus.
The pectinate line of the anal canal, which marks the change from visceral (painless) to somatic (painful) sensory innervation and holds the openings of the anal glands.

sections.title: Appendicitis: obstruction, ischemia, and migrating pain

blocks.text: The appendix is a narrow blind tube arising from the cecum, with a wall rich in lymphoid tissue. Because it has one opening, anything that blocks the lumen turns it into a closed sac. In adults the usual obstruction is a fecalith (a hardened concretion of stool); in children and adolescents it is often hyperplasia of submucosal lymphoid follicles after a viral or bacterial infection. Tumors, such as an appendiceal neuroendocrine tumor, and parasites are rare causes.

Behind the obstruction, mucosa keeps secreting mucus and bacteria keep multiplying, so intraluminal pressure rises. Pressure first collapses thin-walled veins, which causes congestion and edema, and then exceeds arterial inflow, which makes the wall ischemic. Ischemic mucosa loses its barrier, and colonic flora such as Escherichia coli and Bacteroides fragilis invade the wall. Neutrophils infiltrating the muscularis propria are the histologic criterion for acute appendicitis. If the process continues, the wall becomes gangrenous and perforates, usually after about 24 to 48 hours, releasing pus to form a periappendiceal abscess or diffuse peritonitis.

blocks.title: Pathogenesis of acute appendicitis
steps: Fecalith or lymphoid hyperplasia blocks the lumen
Trapped mucus and bacteria raise intraluminal pressure
Venous outflow fails, then arterial inflow fails
Bacteria invade the ischemic wall; neutrophils fill muscularis
Serosa inflames the parietal peritoneum
Gangrene, perforation, abscess, or peritonitis
blocks.caption: Rising pressure in a closed lumen turns obstruction into ischemia, and ischemia lets bacteria cross the wall.

blocks.text: Why the pain moves

Early pain comes from distension of the appendix. Its visceral afferents travel with sympathetic fibers to spinal segment T10, the same segment that supplies the skin around the umbilicus, so the brain refers dull, poorly localized pain to the periumbilical region. Distension also triggers nausea, vomiting, and anorexia through visceral reflexes. Within hours, usually within the first day, inflammation reaches the serosa and touches the parietal peritoneum, which has somatic innervation from the lower intercostal and first lumbar nerves. Pain then becomes sharp and localized at McBurney point, one third of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus, with tenderness, guarding, and rebound.

blocks.caption: Atypical positions (retrocecal, pelvic, or displaced upward in late pregnancy) shift where the parietal peritoneum is irritated, which explains atypical pain sites.

blocks.predict: A patient with 6 hours of vague pain around the umbilicus and vomiting has no right lower quadrant tenderness. Does that rule out appendicitis?
blocks.explain: No. In early appendicitis only the visceral afferents are stimulated, so pain is referred to the T10 dermatome. Localized tenderness appears only when inflammation reaches the somatically innervated parietal peritoneum.
blocks.check: The paragraph on why the pain moves.

blocks.text: The normal esophagus is lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium that meets the columnar gastric mucosa at the squamocolumnar junction, the Z line, near the gastroesophageal junction. Squamous epithelium resists abrasion but not acid, pepsin, and bile. Barrett esophagus is the replacement of distal squamous epithelium by intestinal-type columnar epithelium containing goblet cells, which is intestinal metaplasia. It is an adaptation: columnar cells that secrete mucus survive chronic reflux better than the squamous cells they replace.

The metaplastic cells most likely arise from progenitor cells at the gastroesophageal junction or in esophageal gland ducts that are reprogrammed by repeated injury, with transcription factors such as CDX2 switching on an intestinal program. Endoscopy shows salmon-pink, velvety tongues of mucosa extending up from the gastroesophageal junction into pale squamous mucosa. Segments of 3 cm or more are called long-segment Barrett esophagus and carry higher risk. Biopsy shows columnar epithelium with goblet cells, whose clear mucin vacuoles stain blue with Alcian blue at acid pH.
The dysplasia to adenocarcinoma sequence

Metaplasia itself is not cancer, but the new epithelium proliferates under constant injury and accumulates genetic damage. Early events include loss of CDKN2A (p16); TP53 mutation, aneuploidy, and genomic instability are closely linked to progression to high-grade dysplasia and cancer. Morphologically this appears as low-grade dysplasia, then high-grade dysplasia, then invasive adenocarcinoma of the distal esophagus. Most people with Barrett esophagus never develop cancer, yet their risk is many times that of the general population, and high-grade dysplasia carries a substantial short-term risk of invasion.

blocks.title: Reflux to adenocarcinoma
steps: Chronic acid, pepsin, and bile reflux
Squamous injury: reflux esophagitis
Intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells (Barrett)
Low-grade dysplasia
High-grade dysplasia
Invasive adenocarcinoma of the distal esophagus
blocks.caption: Each step is a histologic stage; only dysplasia and carcinoma are neoplastic.

blocks.title: Esophageal adenocarcinoma versus squamous cell carcinoma
rows: Chronic GERD, obesity, white men, smoking
Smoking, alcohol, hot beverages, nitrosamines, achalasia, caustic injury
blocks.caption: Barrett esophagus explains why adenocarcinoma is distal and why reflux and obesity are its risk factors.

blocks.text: Risk factors for Barrett esophagus are those of long-standing reflux: duration of GERD, central obesity, male sex, white race, older age, and smoking. Many patients have only ordinary heartburn, and some have few symptoms, because the metaplastic lining is less sensitive to acid than squamous mucosa.

A true diverticulum contains all layers of the wall, as in Meckel diverticulum. Colonic diverticula are false diverticula, also called pseudodiverticula: mucosa and submucosa herniate through the muscularis propria and are covered only by serosa. They form at points of weakness where the vasa recta, the small straight arteries supplying the mucosa, pierce the circular muscle, usually in rows between the mesenteric and antimesenteric taeniae.
Why pressure builds in the sigmoid

A low-fiber diet produces small, hard stools. To move them, the colon uses vigorous segmental contractions that close off short chambers, and the pressure inside each chamber rises steeply. The law of Laplace for a cylinder (pressure equals wall tension divided by radius) shows that, for the same wall tension, the narrowest segment develops the highest pressure, and the sigmoid has the smallest diameter. Age-related changes in collagen and elastin weaken the wall further, which is why prevalence rises sharply after 60 years and why connective tissue disorders such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome predispose. In Western populations about 90% or more of diverticula are left-sided, mostly sigmoid; right-sided disease is more common in Asian populations.

blocks.title: Diverticulosis versus diverticulitis
rows: A vas rectum stretched over the dome thins and ruptures into the lumen
Neck obstructed by stool; inflammation and microperforation
Left lower quadrant pain and tenderness
Sudden painless hematochezia, often large and self-limited
Wall thickening and pericolic fat stranding on CT
Abscess, perforation with peritonitis, fistula, stricture
blocks.caption: Bleeding is arterial and painless because it comes from a ruptured vessel without inflammation; pain and fever mean inflammation.

blocks.text: Diverticular bleeding is arterial because the vas rectum, draped over the dome and covered only by mucosa, thins until it ruptures. Inflammation is absent, so there is no pain or fever. Diverticulitis starts when stool obstructs the neck, the trapped sac becomes inflamed, and microperforation lets bacteria into pericolic fat. Because the sigmoid is involved, pain sits in the left lower quadrant, which is why diverticulitis is sometimes called left-sided appendicitis.

When an inflamed segment adheres to a neighboring organ and erodes into it, a fistula forms. A colovesical fistula, the most common, carries gas and stool into the bladder, causing pneumaturia, fecaluria, and recurrent polymicrobial urinary infection; it is more common in men, because in women the uterus lies between the sigmoid and the bladder. Repeated attacks cause fibrosis and stricture with obstruction.

sections.title: Noninfectious enteritis and colitis: radiation, NSAIDs, and microscopic colitis

blocks.text: Not every inflamed bowel is infected or part of inflammatory bowel disease. Radiation, drugs, and immune reactions to luminal antigens injure the mucosa by their own mechanisms, and each leaves a recognizable pattern.
Radiation enteritis and proctitis

Ionizing radiation damages DNA most in rapidly dividing cells, and crypt stem cells renew the intestinal epithelium every few days. Within days to weeks of pelvic or abdominal radiation, crypt cells die, villi shorten, and the surface fails to absorb, causing diarrhea, cramping, and tenesmus. This acute phase usually resolves as surviving stem cells repopulate. Months to years later, a chronic phase appears because radiation also injures small arteries, producing obliterative endarteritis with intimal thickening. Chronic ischemia leads to submucosal fibrosis, strictures with obstruction, ulcers, and fragile mucosal telangiectasias that bleed, most often in the rectum.
NSAID enteropathy and colopathy

NSAIDs injure the small intestine and colon as well as the stomach. Loss of cyclooxygenase-derived prostaglandins reduces mucus, blood flow, and epithelial repair, and the drugs also uncouple mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation in enterocytes and increase mucosal permeability. Bile and bacteria then enter the injured mucosa and cause erosions and ulcers. The result is occult blood loss with iron deficiency anemia, protein loss, and, after repeated healing, thin circumferential fibrous webs called diaphragm strictures, which are characteristic of NSAID injury.
Microscopic colitis

Microscopic colitis causes chronic, watery, nonbloody diarrhea, often with urgency and nocturnal stools, in middle-aged and older adults, more often women. The colon looks normal at colonoscopy, so the diagnosis requires biopsy. It is thought to be an abnormal mucosal immune response to luminal antigens, linked to drugs (NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors, SSRIs) and to autoimmune conditions such as celiac disease and autoimmune thyroid disease. Inflammation and the thickened subepithelial layer impair sodium and water absorption, so diarrhea is secretory in character and persists with fasting in many patients.

blocks.title: Two forms of microscopic colitis
rows: Thick subepithelial collagen band, more than about 10 µm (normal about 3 to 5 µm)
Intraepithelial lymphocytes above about 20 per 100 surface epithelial cells
Lamina propria lymphocytes and plasma cells; surface epithelial damage
Older woman with chronic watery diarrhea
Similar; association with celiac disease is notable
blocks.caption: Biopsy is the only way to make the diagnosis because the mucosa looks normal.

blocks.predict: A 68-year-old woman taking an NSAID and a proton pump inhibitor has 3 months of watery diarrhea without blood, and colonoscopy is normal. What is the most likely finding on random colon biopsies, and why does the colon look normal?
blocks.explain: A thick subepithelial collagen band or excess intraepithelial lymphocytes, indicating microscopic colitis. The disease is confined to the epithelium and lamina propria, without ulcers or erosions, so it changes absorption but not the visible surface.
blocks.check: The microscopic colitis paragraph and table.

sections.title: Peptic ulcer disease: gastric versus duodenal

blocks.text: A peptic ulcer forms when acid and pepsin overcome the mucosal defenses: the mucus and bicarbonate layer, tight junctions, rapid epithelial restitution, and a rich mucosal blood flow that removes back-diffusing acid. Prostaglandins E2 and I2, made by cyclooxygenase, sustain mucus, bicarbonate, and blood flow, and PGE2 also restrains parietal cell acid secretion. Most ulcers are caused by Helicobacter pylori or NSAIDs, and the two act differently.

H. pylori is a curved, flagellated, urease-positive gram-negative rod that lives under the mucus layer. Urease splits urea into ammonia, which buffers acid around the organism and also injures epithelium, while the CagA and VacA proteins drive inflammation. Antral inflammation reduces the number and output of somatostatin-secreting D cells, so G cells lose their brake, gastrin rises, and parietal cells in the healthy body secrete more acid. That acid load reaches the duodenum, which responds with gastric metaplasia that H. pylori can then colonize, producing a duodenal ulcer. NSAIDs act mainly by inhibiting COX-1, which removes prostaglandin protection, and their direct topical injury adds to this; they cause gastric ulcers more often than duodenal ones.

blocks.title: Antral H. pylori and duodenal ulcer
steps: H. pylori colonizes the antrum
Inflammation reduces somatostatin from D cells
G cells released from inhibition: gastrin rises
Parietal cells in the spared body secrete more acid
Acid load causes duodenal gastric metaplasia and ulcer
blocks.caption: Antral infection raises acid; diffuse body infection instead lowers acid and favors gastric ulcer and cancer.

blocks.text: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is caused by a gastrinoma, usually in the duodenum or pancreas and sometimes part of MEN1. Autonomous gastrin causes parietal cell hyperplasia and enormous acid output, giving multiple or refractory ulcers, ulcers in unusual sites such as the distal duodenum and jejunum, and diarrhea because acid inactivates pancreatic lipase and injures the small bowel mucosa.

blocks.title: Gastric versus duodenal ulcer
rows: Lesser curvature, near the antrum and body junction
First part of the duodenum, within a few centimeters of the pylorus
Weak mucosal defense; acid normal or low
Worse with eating; food aversion and weight loss
Eases with eating, returns 2 to 3 hours later and at night
A gastric adenocarcinoma can look like an ulcer, so gastric ulcers are biopsied
blocks.caption: Food buffers acid, which relieves duodenal pain until gastric emptying ends; in the stomach a meal stimulates acid and pepsin onto the ulcer.

blocks.text: Complications follow anatomy

Hemorrhage is the most common complication and presents as hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis, or melena. The gastroduodenal artery runs behind the first part of the duodenum, so a posterior ulcer that erodes it bleeds briskly; a posterior ulcer may also penetrate into the pancreas, causing back pain and raised amylase. An anterior duodenal ulcer, or a gastric ulcer, can instead perforate into the free peritoneal cavity. Air escapes and rises to the highest point, so an upright chest film shows free air under the diaphragm, usually under the right hemidiaphragm. Gastric acid causes chemical peritonitis with sudden severe pain, a rigid abdomen, and sometimes shoulder pain referred through the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5). Scarring at the pylorus can cause gastric outlet obstruction with vomiting of undigested food.

sections.title: Acute erosive gastritis and stress ulcers

blocks.text: Acute gastritis is a transient mucosal inflammation that develops when something abruptly weakens mucosal defense or perfusion. In its severe form, acute erosive hemorrhagic gastritis, the surface shows multiple erosions and petechial hemorrhages. Because erosions stop above the muscularis mucosae, they bleed from capillaries rather than named arteries and heal without scarring if the cause is removed. Patients may have epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting, or present only with hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis, or melena.

blocks.title: Causes of acute erosive gastritis by mechanism
rows: COX-1 inhibition removes prostaglandin support of mucus, bicarbonate, and blood flow; weak acids are trapped and injure epithelial cells directly
Direct toxicity to surface cells, disruption of the mucus barrier, and increased back-diffusion of acid
Splanchnic vasoconstriction causes mucosal ischemia, so bicarbonate delivery and acid removal fail
Ammonia generated from urea inhibits bicarbonate transport into the mucus layer, and uremic toxins injure the mucosa
Direct epithelial injury and impaired renewal
blocks.caption: Every cause either removes a defense or adds an aggressive factor.

blocks.text: Stress ulcers

Stress-related mucosal disease occurs in critically ill patients, particularly those with shock, sepsis, respiratory failure, coagulopathy, burns, or head injury. The central mechanism is mucosal ischemia: low splanchnic perfusion reduces delivery of bicarbonate and removal of back-diffusing hydrogen ions, so epithelial cells become acidotic and die. Stress lesions are usually multiple, shallow, and most common in the acid-secreting body and fundus, and they progress from erosions to ulcers when ischemia persists.

Two named stress ulcers differ in mechanism. A Curling ulcer follows severe burns. Plasma leaks from burned capillaries, causing hypovolemia, and the resulting splanchnic vasoconstriction makes the gastric and proximal duodenal mucosa ischemic; acid output is not the driver. A Cushing ulcer follows intracranial injury, tumor, or surgery. Raised intracranial pressure or direct injury stimulates the vagal nuclei, and vagal acetylcholine drives parietal cells to secrete excess acid. Cushing ulcers occur in the stomach, duodenum, or esophagus and tend to be deeper, so they carry a higher risk of perforation.

blocks.title: Curling versus Cushing ulcer
rows: Not raised; ischemia is the driver
Stomach, duodenum, or esophagus; often deeper
blocks.caption: Curling is a defense failure from low perfusion; Cushing is an aggressive-factor excess from vagal drive.

blocks.text: Normal esophageal squamous epithelium has a basal zone of no more than about 15% of its thickness, and connective tissue papillae that do not reach the upper third of the epithelium. Injury speeds cell turnover, so the basal zone expands and the papillae lengthen. The cause of the injury, however, determines where the lesion is, which cells infiltrate, and what the patient notices.
Reflux esophagitis

Acid and pepsin repeatedly kill surface cells of the distal esophagus. The basal zone expands to more than about 20% of the epithelial thickness (basal cell hyperplasia), papillae extend into the upper third, intercellular spaces dilate, and scattered eosinophils, neutrophils, and lymphocytes enter the epithelium. Changes are greatest just above the gastroesophageal junction, and the typical patient has heartburn and regurgitation.
Eosinophilic esophagitis

Eosinophilic esophagitis is a chronic Th2-mediated allergic disease triggered mainly by food antigens. IL-5 and IL-13 recruit and activate eosinophils, and IL-13 induces epithelial eotaxin-3, which draws in more. Eosinophil granule proteins and TGF-beta cause subepithelial fibrosis and smooth muscle remodeling, so the wall stiffens. Patients are often young men with asthma, eczema, or food allergy, who report solid food dysphagia and food impaction. The diagnosis needs 15 or more intraepithelial eosinophils per high-power field, often with eosinophil microabscesses, and involvement of the proximal as well as distal esophagus. Endoscopy shows concentric rings, longitudinal furrows, and white exudates. Because acid is not the primary cause, reflux control alone often does not normalize the biopsy.
Pill esophagitis

A tablet that lodges in the esophagus dissolves against one patch of mucosa and burns it. Doxycycline and tetracycline are acidic, potassium chloride is hyperosmolar and caustic, NSAIDs act topically and by prostaglandin loss, and bisphosphonates and iron are also common culprits. Pills stick where the esophagus is narrowed by the aortic arch or an enlarged left atrium, especially when taken with little water just before lying down. The patient has sudden odynophagia and retrosternal pain, and endoscopy shows a discrete ulcer with normal mucosa around it.

blocks.title: Distinguishing the three
rows: Basal cell hyperplasia, elongated papillae, few eosinophils
15 or more eosinophils per high-power field, microabscesses
blocks.caption: Eosinophils alone do not separate reflux from eosinophilic esophagitis; density and proximal involvement do.

blocks.predict: A biopsy from the distal esophagus shows 6 eosinophils per high-power field with basal cell hyperplasia, and the proximal biopsy is normal. Which diagnosis fits better?
blocks.explain: Reflux esophagitis. Reflux brings a few eosinophils to the distal epithelium, but eosinophilic esophagitis requires 15 or more per high-power field and usually involves the proximal esophagus as well.

sections.title: Chronic gastritis: H. pylori versus autoimmune

blocks.text: The stomach has two functional zones. The body and fundus contain oxyntic glands with parietal cells, which secrete acid and intrinsic factor, and chief cells, which secrete pepsinogen. The antrum contains G cells that release gastrin and D cells that release somatostatin. The two main chronic gastritides attack opposite zones, which explains why their effects on acid, gastrin, and B12 are opposite.
H. pylori gastritis

H. pylori gastritis is the most common chronic gastritis worldwide. It begins in the antrum, where fewer parietal cells mean a less acidic niche. Histology shows lymphocytes and plasma cells in the lamina propria, neutrophils in the gland necks when the disease is active, lymphoid follicles, and curved rods in the surface mucus. Over decades, inflammation can spread to the body, destroy glands (atrophy), and cause intestinal metaplasia. This multifocal atrophic gastritis is the field in which intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma arises through the sequence inflammation, atrophy, metaplasia, dysplasia, carcinoma. Chronic antigen stimulation also drives B-cell proliferation in the induced lymphoid follicles, which can become extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma; early lesions may regress when the antigen is removed, while those with t(11;18) usually do not.
Autoimmune gastritis

Autoimmune gastritis is caused by CD4 T cells directed against the parietal cell H+/K+ ATPase, accompanied by antibodies to that pump and to intrinsic factor. Parietal cells in the body and fundus are destroyed, while the antrum is spared. Loss of acid removes the negative feedback on antral G cells, so gastrin rises very high; gastrin is trophic to enterochromaffin-like cells, which become hyperplastic and can form gastric neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors. Loss of intrinsic factor prevents ileal absorption of B12, causing pernicious anemia: megaloblastic anemia, glossitis, and subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts. Because acid helps absorb dietary iron, iron deficiency may appear first. The disease is linked to other autoimmune disorders such as Hashimoto thyroiditis and type 1 diabetes, and also raises adenocarcinoma risk.

blocks.title: H. pylori versus autoimmune gastritis
rows: Antrum first, may spread to body
T cells and antibodies against H+/K+ ATPase and intrinsic factor
Normal or raised in antral disease; low if atrophy spreads
Neutrophils in gland necks, lymphoid follicles
Oxyntic gland atrophy, ECL cell hyperplasia
Peptic ulcer, intestinal-type adenocarcinoma, MALT lymphoma
blocks.caption: Which zone is destroyed decides acid, gastrin, and B12 status.

blocks.title: Reading a high gastrin
blocks.text: Two patients have fasting gastrin about 10 times normal. Patient A has gastric pH 7 and a low B12. Patient B has gastric pH 1 and three duodenal ulcers. In A, gastrin is high because acid is absent: parietal cells are gone, so acid no longer triggers antral somatostatin to restrain G cells. This is appropriate secondary hypergastrinemia from autoimmune gastritis, and low B12 reflects lost intrinsic factor. In B, gastrin is high despite strong acid, so the feedback loop is being ignored. That inappropriate, autonomous gastrin points to a gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome). Gastric pH, not the gastrin value alone, separates the two.

The antireflux barrier has three parts. The lower esophageal sphincter (LES) is a 3 to 4 cm zone of tonically contracted smooth muscle with a resting pressure of about 10 to 30 mm Hg above gastric pressure. The right crus of the diaphragm wraps around it and squeezes during inspiration. The intra-abdominal position of the LES and the acute angle of His add a flap valve effect. Once acid does reflux, peristalsis clears the volume and swallowed salivary bicarbonate neutralizes what is left.
Three ways the barrier fails

Transient LES relaxations are the most common mechanism. They are vagovagal reflexes triggered by distension of the gastric fundus, are not preceded by a swallow, and last longer than the brief relaxation that accompanies swallowing; this is why reflux follows large and fatty meals. Low resting LES tone allows free reflux at any time; it occurs with scleroderma, in which smooth muscle fibrosis also weakens peristalsis, and with smoking, alcohol, chocolate, and drugs that relax smooth muscle such as anticholinergics, calcium channel blockers, and nitrates. A sliding hiatal hernia pulls the LES up into the chest, separates it from the crural pinch, and creates a supradiaphragmatic pouch where acid pools and refluxes.

Obesity raises intra-abdominal pressure, which increases the gastroesophageal pressure gradient and promotes hiatal hernia. Pregnancy combines progesterone, which relaxes LES smooth muscle, with upward pressure from the uterus.

blocks.title: From barrier failure to complications
steps: Transient relaxations, low LES tone, or hiatal hernia
Acid, pepsin, and bile reach the esophagus
Clearance fails (supine, weak peristalsis, little saliva)
Squamous injury: reflux esophagitis
Deep ulceration heals by fibrosis: peptic stricture
Chronic injury: Barrett metaplasia
blocks.caption: Reflux injures only when exposure outlasts clearance; complications depend on depth and duration.

blocks.title: Manifestations of GERD and their mechanism
rows: Heartburn, worse after meals, lying down, or bending
Acid stimulates chemoreceptors in the distal esophageal mucosa; posture and gastric distension promote reflux
Microaspiration and an esophagobronchial vagal reflex
Acid and pepsin injure the larynx (laryngopharyngeal reflux)
Esophageal and cardiac afferents converge on the same spinal segments
Peptic stricture: smooth, short, distal fibrotic narrowing
blocks.caption: Extraesophageal symptoms can occur without heartburn.

blocks.text: A peptic stricture forms when ulceration reaches the submucosa and heals by collagen deposition, narrowing the distal lumen and producing slowly progressive dysphagia for solids. Barrett metaplasia (C02) links chronic GERD to esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is chronic, relapsing inflammation that results from an inappropriate mucosal immune response to commensal gut bacteria in a genetically susceptible host, with a defective epithelial barrier. In Crohn disease, loss-of-function variants of NOD2, an intracellular sensor of bacterial peptidoglycan, and of autophagy genes such as ATG16L1 impair the handling of bacteria that cross the epithelium. Macrophages then drive Th1 (interferon gamma) and Th17 (IL-17) responses that organize into granulomas and extend through the wall. Ulcerative colitis (UC) shows a mucosal response with more IL-13 and a defective mucus and epithelial barrier. Smoking raises the risk of Crohn disease but is associated with a lower risk of UC.
Distribution and depth decide everything

Crohn disease can affect any segment from mouth to anus, most often the terminal ileum and proximal colon, with skip lesions of normal bowel between diseased segments, and the rectum is often spared. Inflammation is transmural. Early lesions are aphthous ulcers over lymphoid aggregates that merge into long, knife-like linear fissures; fissures between edematous mucosa create a cobblestone appearance. Mesenteric fat wraps around the serosa (creeping fat), and the thick fibrotic wall narrows the lumen, giving the string sign on barium study. Noncaseating granulomas are characteristic but are found in only a minority of biopsies, so their absence does not exclude Crohn disease. Patients typically have crampy right lower quadrant pain, diarrhea usually without gross blood, weight loss, and perianal disease.

UC always involves the rectum and extends proximally in a continuous pattern, limited to the colon apart from mild backwash ileitis. Inflammation is confined to the mucosa and superficial submucosa. Neutrophils enter crypts (cryptitis) and fill them (crypt abscesses), and chronic injury distorts and branches crypts. Broad ulcers leave islands of regenerating mucosa that stand up as pseudopolyps, and long-standing disease shortens the colon and erases haustra (lead pipe colon). Because the friable mucosa bleeds and the rectum is inflamed, patients have bloody diarrhea with mucus, urgency, and tenesmus.

blocks.title: Crohn disease versus ulcerative colitis
rows: Mouth to anus; terminal ileum most often; rectum often spared
Rectum always, extending proximally in the colon
Cobblestone mucosa, linear fissures, creeping fat, thick wall, strictures
Friable bleeding mucosa, broad ulcers, pseudopolyps, loss of haustra
Crypt abscesses, crypt distortion, no granulomas
blocks.caption: Transmural versus mucosal depth explains most downstream differences, including the complications in C11.

blocks.text: Complications are predictable from two facts in C10: Crohn disease is transmural and favors the terminal ileum, while ulcerative colitis is mucosal and confined to the colon.
Crohn disease: depth and the ileum

Transmural fissures can tunnel through the serosa into an adherent structure, forming fistulas to other loops of bowel (enteroenteric), the bladder (pneumaturia and recurrent infection), the vagina, or the skin, and perianal fistulas and abscesses are common. Repeated transmural inflammation heals by fibrosis, so strictures cause colicky pain and small bowel obstruction. The terminal ileum is the only site that absorbs vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor and that actively reabsorbs conjugated bile acids. Ileal disease or resection therefore causes B12 deficiency with megaloblastic anemia. When less bile acid is lost, the excess entering the colon stimulates chloride and water secretion and causes bile acid diarrhea; when the loss exceeds hepatic synthesis, the bile acid pool shrinks, micelles fail, and steatorrhea follows. A depleted bile acid pool also makes bile supersaturated with cholesterol, causing cholesterol gallstones.

blocks.title: Ileal Crohn disease to calcium oxalate stones
steps: Diseased or resected terminal ileum
Bile acids lost; fat malabsorbed
Fatty acids bind luminal calcium (soaps)
Oxalate left free in the colon
Colonic oxalate absorption rises
Hyperoxaluria: calcium oxalate kidney stones
blocks.caption: Enteric hyperoxaluria needs an intact colon; bile acids and fatty acids also make colonic mucosa more permeable to oxalate.

blocks.text: Ulcerative colitis: the whole colon and the bile ducts

In a severe flare, inflammation can extend into the muscularis propria, and inflammatory mediators such as nitric oxide paralyze colonic smooth muscle. The colon, usually the transverse segment, dilates beyond about 6 cm with fever, tachycardia, and leukocytosis; this toxic megacolon can perforate. Hypokalemia and anticholinergic or opioid drugs worsen the paralysis. Primary sclerosing cholangitis, an immune-mediated concentric onion-skin fibrosis of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts that gives a beaded cholangiogram and cholestatic enzymes, is strongly linked to UC; most patients with it have IBD, while only a few percent of UC patients develop it. It raises the risk of cholangiocarcinoma and of colorectal cancer.
Complications shared by both

Colorectal cancer risk rises with longer duration (from about 8 to 10 years after onset), greater extent of colonic involvement, and coexisting primary sclerosing cholangitis, so it applies to Crohn colitis as well as UC. Chronic inflammation and regeneration drive carcinogenesis from flat dysplasia, with TP53 mutation occurring early and APC loss late, the reverse of the sporadic adenoma to carcinoma sequence.

rows: Tender red nodules on the shins; septal panniculitis
Painful ulcer with undermined violaceous border
Episcleritis parallels activity; uveitis often independent
blocks.caption: All occur in both diseases; primary sclerosing cholangitis is the main extraintestinal link specific to UC.

blocks.title: Why a Crohn patient forms oxalate stones
blocks.text: A man had 120 cm of terminal ileum removed for Crohn disease, keeps an intact colon, and now has steatorrhea and a calcium oxalate kidney stone. Normally, dietary calcium binds oxalate in the gut lumen, forming an insoluble salt that leaves in stool. With the ileum gone, bile acids are lost and the pool shrinks, so fat is not absorbed. Unabsorbed fatty acids bind calcium as soaps, leaving oxalate soluble. Free oxalate, and colonic mucosa made more permeable by bile acids and fatty acids, together raise oxalate absorption and urinary oxalate. Stones form despite normal blood calcium. A patient with an ileostomy and no colon would not develop this mechanism.

Both conditions begin with the same physical event. During forceful retching or vomiting, the abdominal muscles and diaphragm contract forcefully while the lower esophageal sphincter and distal esophagus fail to relax in time. Intragastric pressure surges into an esophagus that has not relaxed, and the wall at and just above the gastroesophageal junction is suddenly stretched. The two syndromes differ only in how deep the wall gives way, and depth predicts every clinical difference.

Mallory-Weiss syndrome is a longitudinal laceration of the mucosa, sometimes reaching the submucosa, at the gastroesophageal junction, usually on the gastric cardia side. Typical settings are binge alcohol use, bulimia, and hyperemesis, and a hiatal hernia predisposes. The tear opens submucosal arteries and veins, so the patient vomits bright red blood after a bout of nonbloody retching. Pain is minimal or absent because the wall is intact, and most tears stop bleeding on their own.

Boerhaave syndrome is a full-thickness, transmural rupture, most often in the left posterolateral wall of the distal esophagus a few centimeters above the junction. This region is weak because its muscle layer is thinner, the esophagus lacks a serosa, and surrounding mediastinal tissue gives little support. Air, gastric acid, food, and bacteria enter the mediastinum. Air dissects along fascial planes into the neck (subcutaneous emphysema, felt as crepitus) and around the heart, where a crunching sound synchronous with the heartbeat (Hamman sign) may be heard. Mediastinal contamination causes chemical then bacterial mediastinitis with severe retrosternal pain, fever, tachycardia, and septic shock. Rupture into the left pleural cavity causes a left effusion containing salivary amylase, low pH, and food particles.

blocks.title: Tear versus rupture
rows: Severe chest or upper abdominal pain after vomiting
Mediastinitis, sepsis, shock; often fatal if unrecognized
Mediastinal air, left effusion, contrast leak on water-soluble esophagram
blocks.caption: Blood without air means a mucosal tear; air without much blood means rupture.

sections.title: Anal fissure, abscess and fistula, proctitis, and rectal prolapse

blocks.text: The dentate (pectinate) line organizes anorectal disease. Above it, the mucosa is columnar and has visceral innervation, so lesions there are relatively painless. Below it, the anoderm is squamous and supplied by the somatic inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve, so lesions there are very painful. The anal crypts and the ducts of the anal glands open at the dentate line, and the internal anal sphincter, a tonically contracted smooth muscle, lies deep to the anoderm.
Anal fissure

An anal fissure is a linear tear of the anoderm below the dentate line, usually caused by passage of a hard stool. About 90% lie in the posterior midline, because the terminal branches of the inferior rectal arteries supply the posterior commissure poorly. Pain makes the internal sphincter go into spasm, the higher pressure compresses those small vessels further, and the ischemic tear fails to heal. The patient has sharp, tearing pain during and after defecation and bright red blood on the paper or stool surface. A chronic fissure shows a sentinel skin tag, a hypertrophied anal papilla, and exposed internal sphincter fibers. A fissure that is lateral, multiple, painless, or unusually large suggests Crohn disease, HIV, syphilis, tuberculosis, or carcinoma.
Abscess and fistula

Most anorectal abscesses are cryptoglandular. An anal gland duct becomes blocked at the dentate line, the gland becomes infected, and pus spreads through the intersphincteric plane to a perianal, ischiorectal, intersphincteric, or supralevator space. The patient has constant throbbing pain, a tender fluctuant swelling, and often fever. When the abscess drains, a persistent epithelialized tract may remain between the internal opening at the crypt and an external opening on the perianal skin; this anal fistula causes chronic intermittent discharge of pus or stool. Crohn disease is the classic cause of complex, multiple, or recurrent fistulas because its transmural inflammation produces them independently of anal glands.

blocks.caption: Fissure and abscess are painful because they involve somatically innervated tissue below the dentate line; an open, draining fistula usually causes discharge more than pain.

blocks.text: Proctitis and rectal prolapse

Proctitis is inflammation limited to the rectal mucosa. An inflamed rectum signals fullness constantly, so patients have tenesmus, urgency, and frequent small passages of mucus and blood. Causes include ulcerative proctitis (UC limited to the rectum), sexually transmitted infections acquired by receptive anal intercourse, Crohn disease, and radiation, as described in C04. Rectal prolapse is protrusion of the full thickness of the rectal wall through the anus. It shows concentric folds, unlike the radial folds of prolapsed hemorrhoids or mucosa. It results from a weak pelvic floor and lax fixation of the rectum, often with pudendal neuropathy from childbirth or chronic straining, and in children it is associated with cystic fibrosis because bulky stools and straining push the rectum out.

integration.text: Across the tube, the same balance decides whether mucosa survives. Aggressive factors include acid and pepsin, bile, drugs, intraluminal pressure, bacteria, and immune effector cells. Defenses include mucus and bicarbonate secreted under prostaglandin control, tight junctions, rapid renewal from stem cells, and above all blood flow. NSAIDs show this at every level, causing gastritis, ulcer, enteropathy, colopathy, and microscopic colitis, and ischemia unites stress ulcers, appendiceal gangrene, radiation stricture, and nonhealing fissures. Anatomy then decides the presentation: depth of injury separates erosion from ulcer, tear from rupture, and UC from Crohn disease; artery position predicts bleeding; and visceral versus somatic innervation predicts pain.

Chronic inflammation is also the bridge to neoplasia. Repeated injury and regeneration select for mutations, which is why Barrett esophagus, atrophic gastritis with intestinal metaplasia, and long-standing colitis precede adenocarcinoma, and why persistent antigen drives MALT lymphoma. The limits of these models matter. Many people with H. pylori, Barrett esophagus, or diverticula never develop disease, symptoms correlate poorly with severity, and histologic thresholds such as eosinophil counts are diagnostic conventions rather than biologic cutoffs.

summary: Appendicitis is obstruction, then rising pressure, ischemia, and bacterial invasion; pain moves from the T10 periumbilical area to McBurney point when the parietal peritoneum is inflamed.
Barrett esophagus is intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells in the distal esophagus from chronic reflux and progresses through low-grade and high-grade dysplasia to adenocarcinoma.
Colonic diverticula are false diverticula where vasa recta pierce the muscle; bleeding is painless and arterial, while diverticulitis causes left lower quadrant pain, fever, abscess, or fistula.
Microscopic colitis causes chronic watery diarrhea with normal-looking mucosa; collagenous colitis has a thick subepithelial collagen band and lymphocytic colitis excess intraepithelial lymphocytes.
Duodenal ulcers come from excess acid (antral H. pylori, gastrinoma) and ease with meals; gastric ulcers come from weak defense, worsen with meals, and are biopsied to exclude cancer.
Posterior duodenal ulcers bleed from the gastroduodenal artery; anterior ulcers perforate and cause free air under the diaphragm.
Curling ulcers follow burns through hypovolemic ischemia; Cushing ulcers follow brain injury through vagal acid hypersecretion.

Autoimmune gastritis destroys body and fundus parietal cells, causing achlorhydria, high gastrin, and pernicious anemia; H. pylori gastritis starts in the antrum and leads to ulcer, adenocarcinoma, and MALT lymphoma.

Crohn disease is transmural, skipping, and granulomatous, causing fistulas, strictures, B12 and bile acid loss, and oxalate stones; UC is continuous and mucosal from the rectum, causing toxic megacolon and linked to primary sclerosing cholangitis.
Mallory-Weiss is a bleeding mucosal tear after retching; Boerhaave is a transmural rupture with pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema.

verify: Timing of appendiceal perforation (often quoted as after about 24 to 48 hours of symptoms) and the share of diverticula that are left-sided in Western populations (about 90% or more) vary between sources.

Definitions of Barrett esophagus differ: US guidelines require goblet cells, while some other guidelines accept columnar metaplasia without them; the long-segment cutoff of 3 cm and annual cancer risk figures also vary. Confirm the definition NABNE uses.
The order of molecular events in Barrett progression (CDKN2A loss early, TP53 mutation with progression to high-grade dysplasia) is simplified here; sources differ on timing.

Histologic thresholds vary slightly: collagen band over 10 µm in collagenous colitis, over 20 intraepithelial lymphocytes per 100 epithelial cells in lymphocytic colitis, basal zone over about 15% to 20% in reflux esophagitis, and 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field in eosinophilic esophagitis.
The share of peptic ulcers attributed to H. pylori has fallen as infection rates drop and NSAID use rises; this chapter states only that H. pylori and NSAIDs cause most ulcers.
The proportion of Crohn biopsies showing granulomas is quoted from about 25% to 50%; this chapter says only that they are found in a minority.
Toxic megacolon is defined by a colonic diameter above about 6 cm with systemic toxicity in most texts; confirm the threshold NABNE uses.
Confirm whether NABNE expects eponyms such as Hamman sign, Rovsing, psoas, and obturator signs, and Goodsall rule for fistula tracts (not included here).
The causes of uremic gastropathy are incompletely defined; the ammonia mechanism given is the usual textbook explanation.
